HOW TO COMPARE
All five screens show the same moment: Spring 1867, season 5 of 20. The post has just arrived — the Weekly reports McCoy buying every board in Abilene, the saloon says a county railroad-bond vote is coming, church talk puts Texas longhorns at $4 a head. Same ledger everywhere: cash $41.50, store tab $28 at 3%/month, cellar ¾, three visits left.

Compare form, not content. Ask of each: Does it read as a game or a lesson? Does information feel like something you go looking for? Does it look like something an 18–25 year old opens on the bus?

A · PLAT MAP — ink on paper, the county as the hub
Motivation: the town is the canary. You literally watch the surveyor's stakes go in and the stockyard appear. Information lives in places you choose to visit.
Tradeoff: a map of squares is quiet. Needs strong scenes inside the buildings to carry emotion.

B · STORYBOOK — painted scenes, narrative first
Motivation: the most emotional read. Choices are people, not tickers. Closest to 80 Days / Reigns, which the audience already knows.
Tradeoff: money can feel like something that happens to you rather than something you manage. Weakest at showing a portfolio.

C · PIXEL FRONTIER — retro pixel art, dialog box, menu
Motivation: instantly reads as a game, and as Oregon Trail specifically — the positioning in one screenshot. Cheapest art pipeline.
Tradeoff: nostalgia may read as a joke to some of the audience; hard to make ledger numbers feel serious in a pixel font.

D · BROADSHEET — the newspaper is the interface
Motivation: information-as-gameplay made literal. Events are headlines, deals are classified ads, prices are the market column, letters home are the correspondence page. Deeply period; nothing else looks like it.
Tradeoff: dense and text-heavy on a phone. The riskiest bet and the most distinctive.

E · TICKERTAPE — contemporary fintech UI, 1867 content
Motivation: looks like the apps the audience already uses for money. The bridge to real life is built into the chrome. Reliability bars make information quality visible.
Tradeoff: loses the period immersion; can feel like a spreadsheet with a hat on. The chart is a spoiler machine.
